newsitem.title: USA: FAA proposes rudder modifications on Boeing 737s.
newsitem.headline: FAA proposes rudder modifications on Boeing 737s.

text.p: U.S. aviation officials on Tuesday proposed modifications to rudders on Boeing 737s to minimize what they said was a small risk of sudden, unexpected rudder movement.
The Federal Aviation Administration said its action was part of a continuing review of the aircraft's flight control system undertaken after two 737s went into uncontrolled rolls and crashed.
Vice President Al Gore said at a safety forum on Jan. 15 that the fixes were developed voluntarily by Boeing Co.. He said the FAA would later order the modifications be made.

Acting FAA Administrator Barry Valentine said the proposed modifications did not represent any conclusion about the cause of the two accidents -- 25 people were killed in the 1991 Colorado Springs crash and 132 in Pittsburgh in 1994.
Despite the unexplained crashes of the two 737s, the plane is still considered one of the world's safest.
The FAA said earlier that the planned fixes would make "a safe plane even safer."
Valentine said the modifications were part of advances made by Boeing for its new 737s and other aircraft models.
He added that the FAA, working with Boeing in the review of the 737 flight control system, would take other actions where warranted, but gave no further details.

The modifications had been recommended by the National Transportation Safety Board, which had called the plane less safe than other craft because of the single rudder valve that could send the plane into a spin and crash.
Investigators said malfunction of the valve was rare.
The directives require replacement of the main 737 rudder power control unit with a new valve designed to end uncommanded rudder motion, including rudder reversal.
The new unit for older planes, required within two years, would be the same Boeing was putting on its new 737s, the FAA said.
It also said it was ordering a modification of the yaw damper, the control that stabilizes a plane in turns and in strong winds, to be fitted within three years.
The FAA earlier recommended new pilot training in how to cope with unexpected rudder movement.

There are about 2,900 Boeing 737s flying worldwide, including about 1,350 flown by U.S. airlines. Boeing estimated the cost of retrofit would be about $126 million worldwide, including about $50 million for those flown by American carriers.
